overview: Cuicuilco was an important early center in the southern Basin of Mexico, now within Mexico City. Its monumental and residential remains belong principally to a much earlier history than this map’s imported 1492 to 1500 interval. The outline locates the archaeological site; it should not be read as an independent fifteenth-century kingdom. Its early urban development preceded Teotihuacan’s regional prominence.

periods.title: Monumental growth in the Preclassic
periods.summary: The great circular platform expanded repeatedly during these approximate centuries. The surviving building incorporates successive construction projects.

periods.title: Changing occupation and a disputed eruption chronology
periods.summary: Studies place the Xitle eruption at substantially different dates around the turn of the era or in later centuries. This broad period brackets competing interpretations; its boundaries are not exact abandonment dates.

periods.title: Later activity and an archaeological landscape
periods.summary: Later visits and occupation left evidence after the major center’s transformation. Lava-covered remains and later construction complicate reconstruction of the ancient settlement.

sections.title: An early center with a distinctive shape

items.text: Cuicuilco occupied a strategic area where streams descended from the Tlalpan uplands. Nearby lakes and oak-pine woodland supplied different resources, while routes connected the basin with the Toluca Valley. Its surroundings help explain why people gathered here.

The great circular platform grew through at least eight enlargements, according to INAH. Its builders packed an earthen core inside a covering of volcanic stone. A monument could be a long series of community building projects rather than one construction day.

A ceremonial structure conventionally called the Kiva preserves red linear decoration made with hematite, an iron-oxide pigment. Andesite slabs and river stones formed its construction. The surviving red lines offer a glimpse of buildings as painted spaces, not simply bare ruins.

Potters made tripod vessels with lids shaped like bird heads. INAH places the ceramic examples it describes within roughly 600 to 200 BCE. Practical containers could be carefully designed objects, with an animal form waiting on top of the lid.

An E1 building burial included pottery, a necklace and two figurines representing a man and a woman. Such a particular set of offerings records choices made for one burial; it does not establish a standard funeral kit for every household.

sections.title: Water, maize and the earth underfoot

items.text: Investigators documented irrigation channels predating the lava. At Cuicuilco D, a reconstructed channel system incorporates smaller channels and a dam. Moving water was part of creating a productive settlement, not merely a concern for its ceremonial buildings.

A 2026 soil study argues that builders selectively dug up, transported and reused older soils near the Estela monument. Microscopic observations, chemistry and conflicting soil ages support that interpretation. Old carbon in reused earth can be older than the building that contains it.

Charred maize plants were found near the great platform and the Estela. Researchers relate the context to agricultural themes in ceremonial life. These traces show maize’s place in the settlement’s material world, although they do not give us a complete family menu.

The Xitle eruption began with ash and later produced lava flows over Cuicuilco and nearby farmland. The damage affected the means of growing food as well as buildings. Geological layers preserve this environmental upheaval even where its exact timing remains debated.

sections.title: Carved signs and an uncertain ending

items.text: The Estela is an andesite column about 3.9 meters tall with carved circles and diamond shapes. Interpretations connect it with ritual or astronomical recording, but the checked research supplies no deciphered sentence. A translated greeting in its builders’ language would be invented.

The date of the eruption remains a research problem. A 2016 archaeomagnetic study proposed roughly 90 BCE to 20 CE; a recent geochemical paper follows radiocarbon recalibrations placing the onset shortly after 380 to 400 CE. These estimates should not be blended into a falsely precise fall year.

Ramírez and Pastrana describe evidence of later visits and some habitation after the eruption. Parts of the landscape that escaped the lava remained usable. The end of Cuicuilco’s greatest importance was therefore different from everyone vanishing permanently from the site.

ending.text: Cuicuilco lost its earlier regional importance, and Xitle lava covered much of its built and agricultural landscape. The precise sequence of decline, eruption and migration remains debated. Later activity continued; neither a single unquestioned fall year nor the map’s 1500 endpoint explains the site’s history.
